variants.name: Non-recursive Mutex/NSLock boundary + private implementation methods
variants.idiom_name: Synchronization.Mutex withLock (or NSLock + defer) + private helpers
variants.implementation_notes: Foundation's NSLock is explicitly non-recursive - Apple's documentation warns that calling lock twice on the same thread locks the thread permanently and points at NSRecursiveLock otherwise - and the newer Synchronization.Mutex provides the same non-recursive exclusive access through a withLock closure, so the classic realization is a public method that locks once (withLock, or lock plus defer unlock) and private methods that assume the lock is held. Apple's guidance is to use a recursive lock when re-entrancy is needed; the cleaner alternative is to drop the lock and let an actor own the state. Keep locks out of async code: blocking a cooperative-pool thread or holding a lock across await is a bug, and the actor variant is how the same component is written for Swift concurrency.
pitfalls: NSLock is not recursive: a second lock() on the same thread hangs forever (Apple documents it), and NSRecursiveLock only hides the double acquisition.
Synchronization.Mutex is non-recursive too, and its withLock closure is not async: never await inside it and never keep the mutex held across a suspension point.
Mixing locks with Swift concurrency blocks a cooperative thread; anything reachable from async code should use actor isolation instead.
The lock must be released from the acquiring thread, so a lock taken in one task and released in another is undefined behaviour.

variants.name: Actor-owned state with private isolated helpers
variants.idiom_name: actor with private helpers assuming isolation
variants.implementation_notes: An actor is Swift's structural answer to the same problem: the state lives in the actor, actor-isolated methods run serialized by the runtime and synchronous internal calls stay inside the same isolation, so there is no lock to re-acquire and the classic interface/implementation split becomes private actor-isolated helpers called from public actor methods. Because actor methods suspend at await and actors are reentrant, invariants must be re-checked after every suspension, and the helpers that never suspend are the ones that may assume isolation. Use the actor variant whenever callers are already async; keep the lock-based variant where the code is synchronous or must interoperate with blocking APIs.
pitfalls: Actor reentrancy: state can change across an await inside an isolated method, so the no-interleaving illusion breaks at suspension points - re-validate after every await.
Blocking calls (locks, semaphores, synchronous I/O) inside an actor stall the cooperative pool; keep actor methods async-friendly.
Synchronous callers cannot await an actor method, and @MainActor is a different isolation domain - bridge the two deliberately instead of mixing them in one component.
